beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Its criticism is therefore not a demand that people stop wanting better lives.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: It asks how a valuable aim changes when it has no stopping condition.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: That question can apply even to aims we ordinarily regard as good.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The chapter on manufactured hunger brings the argument into familiar interfaces.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: A system can answer a need, or continually make another desire salient.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Recommendations observe behavior and then help shape the environment producing that behavior.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The author treats this as a feedback loop, not literal mind control.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Personalization can help people while incentives still reward keeping them engaged.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: A useful question follows about whether products can succeed when their users finish.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The book makes that an institutional design issue rather than a private lifestyle test.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The biological chapters ask what prevents local advantage from damaging a larger system.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Multicellular life depends on constraints that make specialized cooperation possible.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The author uses cancer as a carefully bounded analogy about those constraints failing.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Cells are not moral agents, and societies are not literally bodies.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The text explicitly rejects applying the analogy to peoples or political enemies.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Its narrower question concerns mechanisms that keep successful parts from consuming shared conditions.
